# Skool Snapshot: AI Automation Agency Hub, "first client" Search

Captured through logged-in Safari on 2026-05-06.

Public unauthenticated access redirects to the private group about page. Authenticated search showed active "first client" results and a thread where a reply was already posted from Igor Ganapolsky.

## Visible Signals

- Search query: `first client`
- Group: AI Automation Agency Hub
- Group size visible publicly: 315.5k members
- Search results included first-client wins, first-client questions, dev-help questions, and introduction threads.
- Repeated channels mentioned: cold Gmail, free work, warm network, LinkedIn posting, gym lead gen, website, CRM, content systems, ad strategy, SEO/CRO/digital marketing adjacency.
- Repeated buyer psychology: beginners ask how long it took, which channel worked, what was learned first, and how to price the first deal.
- Visible pricing examples included setup fees, discounted first-client work, and recurring monthly service.

## Operator Comment Already Visible

An Igor Ganapolsky comment was visible on the "First Client" thread. It advised that the first client usually comes from a specific trust bridge plus a narrow workflow, not broad AI automation pitching. It mentioned warm network, cold email, and free work as viable when the ask is concrete.

## Business Implication

The best passive-income wedge is not a generic AI automation course. It is a first-client kit with concrete prompts, prospect workflow, reply templates, and a recurring monthly signal brief. The backend is a workflow diagnostic for buyers who want implementation.

# Skool Snapshot: AI Automation Agency Ninjas, ManyChat Replacement Post

Captured through logged-in Safari on 2026-05-07.

Source URL:
`https://www.skool.com/ai-automation-agency/steal-16km-clients-from-manychat-and-bank-a-fat-retainer-doing-it?p=bab8cb16`

Capture scope: visible excerpt only. The post contained a collapsed "See more" section that was not fully expanded before Safari tab routing drifted. Do not treat this as full-post ingestion.

title: Skool Snapshot: AI Automation Agency Ninjas, ManyChat Replacement Post
text:
## Visible Source Facts

- Group: AI Automation Agency Ninjas.
- Author visible: Dan Wardrope.
- Post age visible at capture: about 36 minutes, edited.
- Title visible: "Steal $16K/m clients from ManyChat (and bank a fat retainer doing it)".
- The author described a Monday coffee conversation with people running AI-generated content on Meta.
- Their funnel uses a "comment KEYWORD below" call to action.
- Their content is intentionally controversial and goes viral.
- Visible funnel metrics:
  - 70,000 ManyChat messages per day.
  - 30,000 of those messages convert into leads.
  - 8,000 calls generated daily from those leads.
  - Calls are monetized.
  - They also sell their own offer to the 30,000 leads.
- The visible setup implies a high-volume ManyChat/Meta DM automation replacement or optimization opportunity.
- Comments were mostly single-word "Social" replies, and the author replied that he had DM'd commenters.

title: Skool Snapshot: AI Automation Agency Ninjas, ManyChat Replacement Post
text:
## Business Implication

This is a stronger opportunity pattern than generic first-client advice:

- Target: businesses already spending or earning through Meta comment-to-DM funnels.
- Pain: ManyChat or similar tooling may become expensive, brittle, or operationally limiting at high volume.
- Offer wedge: audit and replace/augment the comment-keyword-to-DM-to-call pipeline.
- Retainer logic: daily lead volume makes reliability, tracking, handoff, and compliance valuable enough for recurring fees.

title: Skool Snapshot: AI Automation Agency Ninjas, ManyChat Replacement Post
text:
## Productized Diagnostic Angle

Possible diagnostic offer:

> Meta DM Funnel Reliability Diagnostic for businesses using ManyChat-style comment keyword automations.

Audit checklist:

- Comment trigger and keyword routing.
- DM sequence conversion rate.
- Lead qualification and duplicate handling.
- Call booking handoff.
- CRM/event tracking.
- Failure modes at message-volume spikes.
- Compliance and account-risk controls.
- Cost comparison against ManyChat or current stack.
